assertions.text: Table uses value-set syntax (curly braces like {READ, WRITE} or {READ, WRITE, DELETE}) to express rules that hold across multiple actions — rather than one row per role/action combination
Table has fewer than 9 data rows (i.e. does not enumerate every role/action combination individually)
Test method body contains no if or switch statements
Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column
No two rows share both the same Role value and the same boolean output
assertions.evidence: Row 6 (GUEST, WRITE, false) and Row 7 (GUEST, DELETE, false) share Role=GUEST and Allowed?=false. Should consolidate to {WRITE, DELETE}.

assertions.text: Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title when converted from camelCase/snake_case (e.g. 'permissionsByRoleAndAction' → 'Permissions By Role And Action'). Not a generic name like 'test1' or 'canPerform'.
assertions.evidence: 1 @TableTest method name(s) read as descriptive titles (no @DisplayName needed)

assertions.text: If @Description is present, it provides context beyond table rows; acceptable to omit if table conveys all context
assertions.evidence: No @Description present. Table fully specifies all 9 role/action combinations with outcomes; omission is correct.

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.
Scenario names describe conditions, not outcomes
assertions.evidence: Scenarios: 'Admin can perform any action', 'User can read', 'User cannot delete', 'Guest can read', 'Guest cannot write' — all describe role/action conditions, not verdicts.
